<reason>PRO (Side B) held the intuitive high ground with a clean frame ("who writes the rules vs. who appeals them") and a genuinely sharp pressure question about who selects CON's arbitrator. But CON (Side A) did the more damaging work across the exchange. CON answered both pressure questions directly in A1/A2 form and then exploited PRO's own answers: the "unit follows the money" concession shrank the motion's promised representation to two men's sports, and the "decisive" instrument of voluntary conference recognition both made the table contingent on management's permission and, as CON plausibly argued, forfeits the labor-exemption durability PRO had called the round-deciding point. PRO's closing never repaired that collapse; it retreated to the setting-terms frame without addressing the two-sports/permission problem or the immunity-requires-employees rejoinder. PRO also misdescribed the debate by declaring CON "silent" on questions CON had not yet had a turn to answer, an execution error that undercut its weighing. Both sides suffered one clipped turn, roughly cancelling. CON left the judge with a clearer, more grounded comparison: enforceable rights for every athlete now with litigation leverage intact versus a permission-dependent table for a subset that pays for its seat with the leverage that produced every gain.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 turning PRO's Pressure-Question answers against it: the bargaining unit becomes "two men's teams" while the rower organizes "or not," and voluntary recognition means the school decides whether a table exists while a cap signed with non-employees earns no antitrust immunity—dismantling the durability argument PRO had labelled decisive.</best_rebuttal>
